facts.statehood_note: The last state formed entirely east of the Mississippi River.
facts.name_origin: From an Algonquian name for the Wisconsin River. Explorer Jacques Marquette wrote it as "Meskousing" in 1673; the French changed it to "Ouisconsin," and English speakers to "Wisconsin." One leading theory says it comes from a Miami word meaning "it lies red," for the river's red sandstone; Menominee elder Napos Turney suggested the Menominee word Wēskōhsaeh, "good place."

government.chambers: Wisconsin State Senate (33 senators, 4-year terms) and Wisconsin State Assembly (99 representatives, 2-year terms)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term, no term limits); the governor can veto bills and has a line-item veto on spending bills. Other elected officers include the lieutenant governor, secretary of state, treasurer, attorney general, and superintendent of public instruction.
government.courts: Wisconsin Supreme Court (7 justices elected statewide in nonpartisan elections to 10-year terms; only one justice may be elected each year). It meets in the State Capitol.
government.local: 72 counties. Menominee law also applies within the Menominee Indian Reservation.
government.constitution: The original constitution ratified in 1848 is still in use, though it has been amended over a hundred times. Its Declaration of Rights (Article I) bans slavery and guarantees the right to hunt and fish.
government.kid_line: "All people are born equally free and independent, and have certain inherent rights; among these are life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness..." (Wisconsin Constitution, Article I, Section 1)

long_ago.about: Late in the Woodland period (before about 1000 CE), people in southern Wisconsin built thousands of earthen burial mounds in the shapes of animals.
From about 1000 to 1300, a Middle-Mississippian village at Aztalan built large flat-topped pyramid mounds and a stockade (wall) around their village.
A Chiwere-speaking nation whose lands ran south of Green Bay and along rivers to the southwest. The Oneota culture may be ancestors of the Ho-Chunk and Iowa nations.
An Algonquian-speaking nation living in the northeast, with lands beginning north of Green Bay, when Europeans arrived. The Menominee still live in Wisconsin today.
The Ojibwe moved into Wisconsin from the east between 1500 and 1700. Treaties of 1837 and 1842 kept their rights to hunt and fish across their former lands.
The Siouan-speaking Dakota lived in northwestern Wisconsin when Europeans first arrived.

today.about: Federally recognized; Menominee law applies within the Menominee Indian Reservation.
Federally recognized; the Oneida moved to Wisconsin after European contact.

today.nation: Stockbridge-Munsee Community Band of Mohican Indians
today.about: Federally recognized Mohican (Mahican) community, one of the last nations to arrive in Wisconsin.

today.nation: Ojibwe (Lake Superior Chippewa) bands: Bad River Band of Lake Superior Chippewa, Lac Courte Oreilles Band of Lake Superior Chippewa, Lac du Flambeau Band of Lake Superior Chippewa, Red Cliff Band of Lake Superior Chippewa, Sokaogon Chippewa Community (Mole Lake), and St. Croix Chippewa Indians of Wisconsin
today.about: Six federally recognized Lake Superior Chippewa (Ojibwe) bands. In 1983 a federal appeals court (the Voigt decision) affirmed the Lake Superior Chippewa's right to hunt, fish, and gather off-reservation on lands they ceded in treaties.

first_peoples.today_note: Wisconsin has 11 federally recognized tribes: the Menominee, Ho-Chunk, Oneida, Stockbridge-Munsee, Forest County Potawatomi, and six Ojibwe bands. The Brothertown people also remain in Wisconsin. The Sauk, Meskwaki, and Kickapoo, who once lived here, were forced out.
sites: Aztalan State Park: a National Historic Landmark with reconstructed stockade walls and mounds from a village of A.D. 1000–1300
High Cliff State Park: effigy mounds shaped like animals
Lizard Mound County Park: effigy mounds

history.event: The first people (Paleo-Indians) arrive during the Ice Age and hunt animals like mastodons; the Boaz mastodon skeleton was found with spear points in southwest Wisconsin.
In the Woodland period, farming grows and the Effigy Mound culture builds thousands of animal-shaped mounds.
Mississippian people live at the walled village of Aztalan; the Oneota culture also builds large settlements.
French explorer Jean Nicolet canoes west through the Great Lakes, probably the first European to reach Wisconsin, likely landing near Green Bay.
Jacques Marquette and Louis Jolliet travel the Fox-Wisconsin waterway all the way to the Mississippi River. French fur traders work across the region for the next century.
Britain takes control after the French and Indian War. In 1791 two free African Americans set up a fur trading post among the Menominee at today's Marinette.
After treaties push Native nations off land in the southwest, thousands of miners rush in for lead; some live in holes in hillsides, giving Wisconsin the nickname "Badger State."

The Winnebago War (1827) and the Black Hawk War (1832) end with the forced removal of Native nations from most of the state. At the Bad Axe Massacre (August 1–2, 1832), more than 150 Sauk, Meskwaki, and Kickapoo people are killed.
Congress creates Wisconsin Territory on April 20.
Wisconsin becomes the 30th state on May 29 as a free state.

Freedom seeker Joshua Glover is seized near Racine under the Fugitive Slave Act; in March a crowd breaks him out of the Milwaukee jail, and he escapes to Canada. The Wisconsin Supreme Court later declares the Fugitive Slave Law unconstitutional. The Republican Party is founded in Ripon.
About 91,000 Wisconsin soldiers fight for the Union, including the Iron Brigade regiments and the 8th Wisconsin with its eagle mascot, Old Abe.

Ezekiel Gillespie, a Black Milwaukee leader, is refused a ballot in 1865 and sues. In 1866, in Gillespie v. Palmer, the Wisconsin Supreme Court rules unanimously for him, agreeing that voters had approved Black men's right to vote in an 1849 referendum.

trailblazers.name: Electa Quinney
trailblazers.text: Electa Quinney, a Mohican woman of the Stockbridge-Munsee Community, opened a school at Statesburg by 1828 and taught 40 to 50 students. It is called the first public school in Wisconsin, making her the first woman to teach in a public school there. A statue of her stands in Kaukauna.

trailblazers.name: Ezekiel Gillespie
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved, Ezekiel Gillespie bought his own freedom and moved to Milwaukee, where he helped run the Underground Railroad and helped start Wisconsin's first African American church. When he was refused a ballot in 1865, he sued, and in 1866, in Gillespie v. Palmer, the Wisconsin Supreme Court ruled unanimously that Black men in Wisconsin had the right to vote.

trailblazers.name: Cordelia Harvey
trailblazers.text: After her husband, Governor Louis Harvey, drowned in 1862 while visiting wounded soldiers, Cordelia Harvey cared for sick Wisconsin soldiers in Union hospitals. She kept pressing President Lincoln in person until he agreed to build hospitals away from the battlefront; three were built in Wisconsin. Soldiers called her the "Wisconsin Angel."

trailblazers.name: Mountain Wolf Woman (Xéhachiwinga)
trailblazers.text: Mountain Wolf Woman was born into the Thunder Clan near Black River Falls. Her autobiography is one of the earliest firsthand accounts of the life of a Native American woman.

trailblazers.name: Vel Phillips
trailblazers.text: Vel Phillips of Milwaukee was the first African American woman to graduate from the University of Wisconsin Law School. In 1956 she became the first woman and first African American on the Milwaukee Common Council, and she fought for fair housing. In 1978 she became the first woman and first person of color elected Wisconsin's secretary of state.

trailblazers.name: Ada Deer
trailblazers.text: Born in Keshena on the Menominee Reservation, Ada Deer was the first Menominee to earn a bachelor's degree from the University of Wisconsin (1957). She led the fight that won the Menominee Restoration Act of 1973, which restored federal recognition to the Menominee, and chaired the Menominee Restoration Committee. In 1993 she became the first woman to lead the Bureau of Indian Affairs as Assistant Secretary of the Interior.

landforms: Northern Highland, with Timms Hill, the highest point (1,952 feet)
Central Plain and the sandstone Dells of the Wisconsin River
Eastern Ridges and Lowlands, including the Niagara Escarpment
Western Upland and the Driftless Area, with Mississippi River bluffs and the Baraboo Range
Apostle Islands and the Door Peninsula
geography.regions: Wisconsin has five natural regions: the Lake Superior Lowland, the Northern Highland, the Central Plain, the Eastern Ridges and Lowlands, and the Western Upland.

ecosystems.name: Northern forests and glacial lakes
ecosystems.about: The Northern Highland holds huge mixed hardwood and conifer forests, including the 1.5-million-acre Chequamegon–Nicolet National Forest, and thousands of glacial lakes. Wolves grew from 0 to about 6,000 by 2023, and elk brought back in 1995 now number over 400.

ecosystems.name: Great Lakes shores
ecosystems.about: Wisconsin has the third-longest Great Lakes coastline. Sea caves line the shores of the Apostle Islands in Lake Superior.

ecosystems.name: Driftless Area hills and bluffs
ecosystems.about: This southwest region was not covered by glaciers in the last ice age, so it has steep bluffs carved by meltwater instead of flat glacial land.

ecosystems.name: Rivers and wetlands
ecosystems.about: More than 12,000 named rivers and streams flow through the state. Bald eagles, once rare, are now seen in nearly every county.

science.weather: Cold, snowy winters and warm summers. Snowfall averages about 40 inches in the south and up to 160 inches a year in the Lake Superior snowbelt. The record low was −55°F at Couderay in 1996, and the record high was 114°F in Wisconsin Dells in 1936. Severe storms, floods, and droughts have been increasing.
science.resources: America's Dairyland is famous for milk and cheese. Wisconsin grows more than half the nation's cranberries and 97% of its ginseng, leads the nation in paper products, and has big manufacturing, health care, and technology industries; lead was mined in the 1800s.
science.highlight: The Driftless Area of southwest Wisconsin was not covered by glaciers in the last ice age, so instead of flat glacial land it has rugged bluffs carved by water from melting glaciers. Much of the rest of the state is dotted with thousands of glacial lakes.

g3_ss.title: Wisconsin Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Electa Quinney, Ezekiel Gillespie, Cordelia Harvey, Mountain Wolf Woman, and Vel Phillips; students act out one moment from each life.

g45_ss.title: Wisconsin's First Nations

g45_ss.title: Fur Trade to Lead Rush
g45_ss.plan: Nicolet, Marquette and Jolliet, French and British fur trade, the 1791 Black traders at Marinette, lead mining, and the Black Hawk War and removals.

g45_ss.title: Free State, 1848–1877

g3_sci.plan: Dairy cows, cranberry bogs, and maple trees; trace milk from farm to cheese.
